     - Returns a dict: {"ended_reason": "checkpoint"|"exception"|"quota", "continuation_summary_path": str, "real_actions_taken": int}.

Write a function `promote_checkpoint_if_strictly_better(metrics_before: dict, metrics_after: dict) -> bool` that only moves `frankenstein-checkpoint-current` forward to the new commit if EVERY key in metrics_after is equal-or-better than the corresponding key in metrics_before (define "better" directionally per metric name, e.g. latency/RAM/error-count should go DOWN, throughput should go UP -- take a metric_directions dict as a parameter rather than hardcoding assumptions) -- if even ONE metric regressed, return False and leave the checkpoint tag where it was (the candidate commit still exists in history, just not referenced by the checkpoint tag). Write `rollback_to_last_checkpoint()` and `rollback_to_ur_baseline()` as two clearly distinct functions (not the same function with a flag) so the two rollback levels are unambiguous in the code and in any logs.
   - Writes its findings back into the shared "frankenstein:build_state" fabric scope (so the Bauleiter can see what was fixed) via the same coordinator_commit path already used everywhere else.

Write both scripts as real, runnable Python (not pseudocode). Neither will be executed by you (no live model/API access in your sandbox for the actual 72h run) -- write them to be correct by careful reading of the actual APIs involved (grid10_fabric.py, llm.py, harness_aider.py's actual CLI), and write companion test files that test the NON-networked logic in isolation (e.g. the continuation-context framing text construction, the state-fabric task-tracking calls against a real tmp Fabric instance, the rate-limit backoff timing logic, the bugfix git-rollback mechanism against a real tmp git repo) -- mock/stub anything that would need a real network call.
